answer.label: Not Karl Marx — an anonymous line, first documented in 2008
answer.authorDates: First documented 23 December 2008 · spread by email and blog comment during the financial crisis
answer.sourceLine: Marx did not write this. The earliest documented appearance is a reader comment signed “Gpkkid,” posted on 23 December 2008 in the comment thread of the New York Times Economix blog ↗ and credited only to “Karl Marx, 1867” — no book named. Snopes rates the Das Kapital attribution False ↗, and Wikiquote files the line under Misattributed ↗.

source.excerpt:
“Owners of capital will stimulate working class to buy more and more of expensive goods, houses and technology, pushing them to take more and more expensive credits, until their debt becomes unbearable.

The unpaid debt will lead to bankruptcy of banks which will have to be nationalized and State will have to take the road which will eventually lead to communism.” – Karl Marx, 1867
trail: 23 December 2008 — the earliest documented appearance. A reader signed “Gpkkid” posts the lines, credited simply to “Karl Marx, 1867,” in the comments on Utpal Bhattacharya’s Economix post “Do Bailouts Encourage Ponzi Schemes?” ↗. No source work is named.

14 January 2009 — now tagged “Das Kapital, 1867,” the quote is circulating on Wall Street. Megan McArdle calls it fake in The Atlantic ↗: Marx’s thesis was that falling wages would immiserate the working class, not that workers would be done in by their overdrafts.

4 February 2009 — the ClockBackward essay ↗ runs thirteen separate searches of the Marx/Engels Collected Works and finds nothing resembling either variant; a week later the Los Angeles Times calls it a hoax quote ↗.
21 April 2009 — Snopes publishes its verdict: False ↗. Wikiquote has kept the line in its Misattributed section ever since ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest documented form, quoted exactly as it was posted. Note what is missing: no book, no chapter, no translator — just a name and a year. Every later version adds specificity the original never had, and the wording itself keeps drifting (“nationalized” becomes “nationalised,” “technology” becomes “technological products”), which is how anonymous forwards behave and is not how a printed translation behaves.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for this wording, because no source work exists for it: the earliest documented instance is an anonymous 2008 comment, and no manuscript, edition or translation has ever been produced. The book it is falsely credited to is a separate matter — <cite>Das Kapital</cite>, Volume I was published in German in 1867 and in English in 1887 in Samuel Moore and Edward Aveling’s translation, both long in the public domain — but that has no bearing here, since the sentences are not in it.

author.heading: Who Marx actually was
author.metaLine: 1818–1883 · German philosopher, economist and author of Das Kapital
author.bio: Karl Heinrich Marx (5 May 1818 – 14 March 1883) was a German philosopher, economist and revolutionary socialist whose first volume of Das Kapital appeared in German in 1867; the later volumes were completed after his death by Friedrich Engels. His argument there is that competition drives capitalists to squeeze wages and lengthen hours, immiserating the working class — not that workers would be undone by their own borrowing. Marx wrote at length about the wretched housing available to workers, and he used the word technology in the sense of the study of industrial processes, not of consumer goods on credit.

misattribution.heading: What gets claimed, and what the record shows
misattribution.intro: This is one of the crisis era’s most successful fabrications: a paragraph of modern economics dressed in a nineteenth-century name. Three separate claims travel with it, and all three fail.

items.why: Snopes rates it False ↗, reporting that searches of Marx’s works for the German equivalents of the less common words here — “bankruptcy,” “technology,” “unbearable” — turn up no matching passage. Wikiquote lists the line under Misattributed ↗.

The earliest documented instance credits only “Karl Marx, 1867” with no book named; within days the “Das Kapital, 1867” tag was attached, and it is that version Megan McArdle quoted on 14 January 2009 ↗ as it circulated on Wall Street. The distinctive strings “bankruptcy of banks,” “expensive credits” and “eventually lead to communism” do not occur anywhere in the Moore and Aveling English text of Capital, Volume I ↗.

A NewsMutiny spoof about Americans being sent back to preschool ↗ quotes a looser variant — “condos… technological products… the pathway to communism.” Some readers concluded the site had invented it, but the essayist who contacted its author ↗ was told plainly that he had received one of the emails himself and had not written the quote.

misattribution.truthLine: No one has produced a manuscript, letter, edition or translation containing these sentences. The whole documented life of the quote begins in a comment box on a New York Times blog in December 2008 ↗, and the burden of proof has stayed with the believers ever since.

context.heading: Why a fake Marx quote was irresistible in 2009
lead: The lines surfaced in the worst weeks of the financial crisis, days after the Madoff fraud broke and months after governments began taking banks onto their own balance sheets. Read in that moment, the passage looked like a dead economist calling the score in advance: mortgages, consumer credit, bank failure, nationalisation. It travelled by email, then by trading-desk forward, and by mid-January 2009 Megan McArdle was reporting that it was “making the rounds of Wall Street” ↗ with “Das Kapital, 1867” attached.

What gave it away was the economics, not the prose. Marx’s case was that competition forces wages down and ruins workers as producers; a story in which workers ruin themselves as over-extended borrowers, and in which the state walks calmly down a road to communism rather than being overthrown, belongs to a much later argument. The Los Angeles Times called it a hoax quote in February 2009 ↗, and nobody who went looking has produced the passage since.
detailsBody: McArdle’s objection was that ordinary working people of Marx’s day simply had no access to bank credit. They might run up an account with a landlord or a butcher, but the first mass extension of credit to people who owned no land was the instalment-buying boom of the 1920s — long after Marx died. A prophecy about households taking “more and more expensive credits” has no nineteenth-century object to describe.

One popular objection does not hold up, and it is worth retiring. Sceptics often say the word “technology” is anachronistic for Marx. It is not: the ClockBackward essay found he discussed technology and technological change with some frequency, and the term appears in the Moore and Aveling English text of <cite>Capital</cite>, Volume I — where Marx calls for “a critical history of technology” and says technology “discloses man’s mode of dealing with Nature.” That is the study of industrial processes, not gadgets bought on credit. The quote fails on its argument and on its documentary record, which is a far stronger case than a vocabulary hunch.
context.pull: “If only he had actually said it, Americans might have a healthy new respect for — or maybe fear of — Karl Marx.” — Tom Petruno, Los Angeles Times, 11 February 2009

sourcesVerified.claim: Snopes rates the claim that this passage comes from Marx's Das Kapital as False, published 21 April 2009 by David Mikkelson; says the earliest reference found was a December 2008 blog post; searches for German equivalents of 'bankruptcy', 'technology', 'unbearable' found no matching passages; quotes David Wighton (London Times) and Megan McArdle.

Wikiquote's Karl Marx page lists this quote in its Misattributed section, notes it was said to be from Das Kapital in an anonymous email, cites the Snopes debunking, and names the earliest occurrence found as a post by Gpkkid on 23 December 2008; also notes the NewsMutiny satirical article and that its author says he is not the author of the quote.

The New York Times Economix post 'Do Bailouts Encourage Ponzi Schemes?' by Utpal Bhattacharya, 18 December 2008, carries a comment by 'Gpkkid' dated December 23, 2008, 8:19 am containing the quote credited to 'Karl Marx, 1867' with no book named.

The ClockBackward essay of 4 February 2009 ran thirteen listed searches of the Marx/Engels Collected Works on marxists.org and found nothing resembling the quote; it traced a variant to the satire site NewsMutiny; and in an update the NewsMutiny article's creator states 'I didn't invent it. I got one of those emails myself.' It also notes that Marx did discuss technology with some frequency.

Megan McArdle's post 'Faux Marx', dated 14 Jan 2009, quotes the passage as attributed to 'Karl Marx, Das Kapital, 1867', says it is making the rounds of Wall Street, and argues it is fake because Marx's core thesis was that falling wages would immiserate the working class and because no one in that era imagined the working class having access to bank credit — the first mass extension of credit to people who did not own land being the 1920s instalment-buying boom.

The Los Angeles Times 'Money & Company' post by Tom Petruno, dated Feb. 11, 2009, calls it a hoax quote circulating on the Internet attributed to Marx, says no one who has looked into it has found any such actual quote from Marx, and cannot find it on marxists.org.

Marxists.org hosts Capital: Volume One by Karl Marx, first published in German in 1867, first published in English in 1887, translated by Samuel Moore and Edward Aveling and edited by Frederick Engels. The strings 'bankruptcy of banks', 'expensive credits' and 'eventually lead to communism' do not appear in its chapter texts, though 'owners of capital' does occur once, in Chapter 33, inside Marx's quotation of E. G. Wakefield; Chapter 15 does contain Marx's remarks calling for 'a critical history of technology' and saying technology 'discloses man's mode of dealing with Nature'.

The NewsMutiny satire 'Americans to Undergo Preschool Reeducation in Advance of Country's Conversion to Communism' cites Karl Marx as having presaged: 'The owners of capital will stimulate the need of the working class to take expensive, collateral loans to buy their condos, houses and technological products; and, at the end, these unpaid debts will result in the nationalization of the banks upon their bankrupcy, and so the state will be on the pathway to communism.'

Karl Heinrich Marx was a German philosopher and economist; Wikiquote's biographical header gives his dates as 5 May 1818 – 14 March 1883 and states he published the first volume of Das Kapital in 1867, the two later volumes being completed by Friedrich Engels.
